scenario.title: PendSV priority not lowest - the context switch runs inside an interrupt handler
scenario.description: The kernel from P06 plus a long button interrupt handler (priority 0xC0, less urgent than SysTick at 0x80). The handler counts to 3000 in r4 with a shadow copy in r5 and checks that they still agree at the end. SysTick ticks while the handler runs and pends PendSV. In the "correct" variant PendSV has the lowest priority (0xFF), so it waits until the button handler has returned and then switches tasks cleanly. In "pendsv_high" PendSV was given 0x80, the same as SysTick: it pre-empts the button handler, saves the handler's registers as if they were the task's, loads another task's registers and returns into the handler. The handler continues with another task's r4/r5, and the interrupted tasks resume with mixed-up registers.

variants.name: pendsv_high
variants.hidden_symptom: Under button presses, a long interrupt handler occasionally computes a wrong result and a task's counter jumps; with no button presses everything is fine.

expected.summary: With PendSV lowest, the button handler always finishes intact and every switch happens with EXC_RETURN 0xFFFFFFFD; with PendSV at 0x80, switches run on top of the handler (EXC_RETURN 0xFFFFFFF1) and the handler detects corrupted registers.

scenario.what_to_look_for: Both variants: two button presses, each an exception_entry for IRQ_GPIO from a task, and SysTick ticks that pre-empt the long handler (exception entries with EXC_RETURN 0xFFFFFFF1, i.e. "I interrupted a handler"). In "correct" the irq_pend PendSV stays pending until the button handler's exception_return, then PendSV tail-chains with LR=0xFFFFFFFD and the switch is clean. In "pendsv_high" the kernel event at init already warns that PendSV is not the lowest priority; then the SysTick return tail-chains straight into PendSV with LR=0xFFFFFFF1 and the context_switch event warns "running ... on top of another handler". A marker "GPIO handler: r4/r5 changed under the handler" follows, and isr_corruptions counts it. Click the context_switch in the viewer and compare the saved r4/r5 of the switched-out task with the handler's loop counter.
likely_root_causes: PendSV priority left at its reset value 0 (the most urgent configurable level) because SHPR3 was never written.
SHPR3 written as a whole word with the wrong byte order, so PendSV got SysTick's priority or vice versa.
All system exceptions set to one 'kernel priority' for convenience, so PendSV ties with or beats device interrupts.
A kernel that triggers the switch directly from SysTick or an ISR instead of pending PendSV.
how_to_debug: Read SHPR3 in GDB: 'x/xw 0xE000ED20'. Byte 2 (PendSV) must be the numerically largest priority in the system (0xF0 with 4 priority bits).
In PendSV_Handler assert that LR == 0xFFFFFFFD (or check EXC_RETURN bit 3 = thread mode); halt if not.
Put a marker pin in the long ISR and another in PendSV: on the scope a PendSV pulse inside the ISR pulse is the bug.
In the ISR, keep a shadow copy of a callee-saved register as here and check it at the end; corruption that appears only under interrupt load points at the switch.
scenario.what_this_means: PendSV is lowest priority by design: it makes the switch wait until every other handler has finished, so the only thing it ever saves is a task. Give it a higher priority and the kernel will one day save an interrupt handler's registers into a task's context. Nothing faults; registers just move between contexts, which is the hardest kind of bug to find without knowing this rule.
scenario.hidden_symptom: Under button presses, a long interrupt handler occasionally computes a wrong result and a task's counter jumps; with no button presses everything is fine.
